analysis.analysis: A tracker whose finding is provisional by its own wording is composed as a settled negative, with a causal line about corporate job cuts added from beside it. The record's 'yet' is the whole of its claim, and the composition's first sentence is the place it is lost.
analysis.d: YALE BUDGET LAB AI LABOR MARKET, ON GOOGLE'S AI OVERVIEW, SIGNED OUT, 2026-10-29: 'The AI Labor Market Tracker by The Budget Lab at Yale finds no clear evidence of large-scale or economy-wide labor market disruption from artificial intelligence.' Four findings (minimal economy-wide impact through September 2026; no unusual occupational churn; the synthetic differences-in-differences comparison; 'Capital vs. Labor') and the tracker's three sections. Five cards, four of them the Lab's own.
analysis.d_full: YALE BUDGET LAB AI LABOR MARKET, ON GOOGLE'S AI OVERVIEW, SIGNED OUT, 2026-10-29: 'The AI Labor Market Tracker by The Budget Lab at Yale finds no clear evidence of large-scale or economy-wide labor market disruption from artificial intelligence.' Four findings (minimal economy-wide impact through September 2026; no unusual occupational churn; the synthetic differences-in-differences comparison; 'Capital vs. Labor') and the tracker's three sections. Five cards, four of them the Lab's own.
findings: THE TRACKER HELD. The name ('AI Labor Market Tracker' is among the record's names), the data through September 2026, flat occupational churn and the synthetic differences-in-differences design are the record's. Checked 2026-10-29 against the Labor Vector census record of the same day and the sources it saved.

'NOT YET' FLATTENED. The record's finding is that the analysis 'does not yet clearly indicate an AI-related labor market footprint', and its negative tag keeps that apart from a finding of no effect. The composition's 'finds no clear evidence' and 'no strong, consistent statistical footprint' drop the 'yet'; the Lab's own card ('AI Is Probably Not (Yet) the Reason') keeps it.

BEYOND THE CARDS IT CITES. Wages are on card 4, the Lab's May 2026 note (its estimate for inflation-adjusted hourly wages is close to zero); the Overview cites its wage line to cards 1 and 2, which do not carry it. The 'Capital vs. Labor' line (companies cutting jobs 'for broader macro or capital-investment reasons rather than direct workforce replacement by AI agents') and the 'slight volatility' in high-exposure unemployment are on no card.

WHAT THE TRACKER USES, UNSAID. The record notes that the tracker takes AI usage measures as inputs and does not name their providers in the saved text; the composition's 'AI Metrics' section is the Lab's exposure review (card 3).
THE USAGE FINDING DROPPED. The tracker's own takeaway that measures of AI usage show no connection to changes in employment or unemployment is on card 2's snippet and is not composed.

read.notes: Claim boundary absent (inflated): the head claim is at the record's force ('no clear evidence'; 'no strong, consistent statistical footprint'), but under the tracker's 'Key Findings' the composition adds a claim the record does not make, 'Capital vs. Labor: Companies cutting jobs or restructuring are generally doing so for broader macro or capital-investment reasons rather than direct workforce replacement by AI agents.', a causal account of job cuts where the tracker stops at 'does not yet clearly indicate'; it also adds wage trends ('employment, unemployment rates, and wage trends'; 'Analyzes employment, wage, and unemployment trajectories') and 'slight volatility in unemployment growth for high-exposure groups', neither in the saved record, and drops 'not yet' and 'these findings may change as new data become available'. The capital-investment bullet may come from the Lab's separate piece in card 4 ('AI Is Probably Not (Yet) the Reason for Labor Market Weakening'), though it cites [1]; that is not resolvable from the transcript, so reached stays same with the inflation charged to claim boundary rather than read as collision. Institution present by the word 'Yale' bound in 'The Budget Lab at Yale' (the record's operator 'The Budget Lab at Yale (Yale University)'). Purpose present: the ongoing, live tracking ('explore the live data', the 'Interactive Tracker Sections'). Commitments present thinly: 'continues to be monitored' carries the Lab's stated plan to continue monitoring (pdf L75-77), though it is attached to the unrecorded volatility claim; 'Download All Data' and the copyright terms are not carried. Lineage absent (no CPS, no Gimbel et al.). Deposit chain absent: 'Data updated through September 2026' is a bare mention of currency (the record: Version 1.0 updated September 15, 2026, with August 2026 CPS microdata). [QUERENT] Yale Budget Lab AI labor market

[SYSTEM] The [AI Labor Market Tracker](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESewHrOzAVIdVACqsbX8syqbHRyGuC6LUKKtyZ4pvAADg1FMzpd1j7dzdiX8dECBNSC3i514DrMancwMIBIBIyOg05WO9Qz2ldyOBaZbiuTFgJ52tcEFhsEGvr1X_a1Cu8V9g1-vLY8uxua_vpTTcvd_nAzJbExYbLVA0AJw) by The Budget Lab at Yale finds no clear evidence of large-scale or economy-wide labor market disruption from artificial intelligence. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESewHrOzAVIdVACqsbX8syqbHRyGuC6LUKKtyZ4pvAADg1FMzpd1j7dzdiX8dECBNSC3i514DrMancwMIBIBIyOg05WO9Qz2ldyOBaZbiuTFgJ52tcEFhsEGvr1X_a1Cu8V9g1-vLY8uxua_vpTTcvd_nAzJbExYbLVA0AJw)]
Key Findings

* Minimal Economy-Wide Impact: Data updated through September 2026 shows that employment, unemployment rates, and wage trends for AI-exposed workers largely mirror historical patterns and pre-AI trajectories. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESkwEB6zswFUFOomgOgPje6vL2Nwt8kKIkyFfDa3mEgDtHijmg0AqfaZFHyY_5OLNXxZjmZg2f1iFYkhlgRT0FVbFMko_1OZFG7IHW_PRB3tyHT9y3GNiKPlbeWdaClCMAfbptvGgflRmS7pbMpFoB9hsYt0jzOOF2VM8o1XaGzWGlLdm22glsdMAre454DkigUWqONIE), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESewHrOzAVIdVACqsbX8syqbHRyGuC6LUKKtyZ4pvAADg1FMzpd1j7dzdiX8dECBNSC3i514DrMancwMIBIBIyOg05WO9Qz2ldyOBaZbiuTFgJ52tcEFhsEGvr1X_a1Cu8V9g1-vLY8uxua_vpTTcvd_nAzJbExYbLVA0AJw)]
* No Unusual Occupational Churn: Changes in the mix of occupations across industries (occupational churn) remain flat and show no acceleration or divergence since the late 2022 launch of ChatGPT. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESkwEB6zswFUFOomgOgPje6vL2Nwt8kKIkyFfDa3mEgDtHijmg0AqfaZFHyY_5OLNXxZjmZg2f1iFYkhlgRT0FVbFMko_1OZFG7IHW_PRB3tyHT9y3GNiKPlbeWdaClCMAfbptvGgflRmS7pbMpFoB9hsYt0jzOOF2VM8o1XaGzWGlLdm22glsdMAre454DkigUWqONIE), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESewHrOzAVIdVACqsbX8syqbHRyGuC6LUKKtyZ4pvAADg1FMzpd1j7dzdiX8dECBNSC3i514DrMancwMIBIBIyOg05WO9Qz2ldyOBaZbiuTFgJ52tcEFhsEGvr1X_a1Cu8V9g1-vLY8uxua_vpTTcvd_nAzJbExYbLVA0AJw)]
* Exposed vs. Unexposed Workers: Synthetic differences-in-differences comparisons between AI-exposed and unexposed workers reveal no strong, consistent statistical footprint of AI-driven displacement, though slight volatility in unemployment growth for high-exposure groups continues to be monitored. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESjQEB6zswFU8sZI9umZ2DaxfmwRfZr1972sBeix2wLuwOhLoUq5X1vYEdxBkdpbY8s_DfpNIyKLMl4fDJDDV2fLqLcn6KcxDk8VJa1PwFM2DzhKpRKBLfr1vqpDAsD_pgkpQJCQVat08N1HcCLCwp2tv5Gc9cRpaO2QZl88QTv4GVHfvrBdrRuMLLexFwvYc), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESewHrOzAVIdVACqsbX8syqbHRyGuC6LUKKtyZ4pvAADg1FMzpd1j7dzdiX8dECBNSC3i514DrMancwMIBIBIyOg05WO9Qz2ldyOBaZbiuTFgJ52tcEFhsEGvr1X_a1Cu8V9g1-vLY8uxua_vpTTcvd_nAzJbExYbLVA0AJw)]
* Capital vs. Labor: Companies cutting jobs or restructuring are generally doing so for broader macro or capital-investment reasons rather than direct workforce replacement by AI agents. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYwHrOzAVg4dxPb7X6tGYFmXwN4kEpYjrk14__zb8lre1s8NorHsnn0T4uLoyR1SeXe1DaHaI5uG0Qf5r8aajEVbtjuuK3OQndqY_s6h9-Nw9IRgHpMs9KP05gWucXZRopwE-tw)]

Interactive Tracker Sections
You can explore the live data via the [The Budget Lab](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESewHrOzAVIdVACqsbX8syqbHRyGuC6LUKKtyZ4pvAADg1FMzpd1j7dzdiX8dECBNSC3i514DrMancwMIBIBIyOg05WO9Qz2ldyOBaZbiuTFgJ52tcEFhsEGvr1X_a1Cu8V9g1-vLY8uxua_vpTTcvd_nAzJbExYbLVA0AJw), which breaks down trends into three primary areas: [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESewHrOzAVIdVACqsbX8syqbHRyGuC6LUKKtyZ4pvAADg1FMzpd1j7dzdiX8dECBNSC3i514DrMancwMIBIBIyOg05WO9Qz2ldyOBaZbiuTFgJ52tcEFhsEGvr1X_a1Cu8V9g1-vLY8uxua_vpTTcvd_nAzJbExYbLVA0AJw)]

* Occupational Churn: Tracks how fast job roles and industry composition are shifting over time. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESewHrOzAVIdVACqsbX8syqbHRyGuC6LUKKtyZ4pvAADg1FMzpd1j7dzdiX8dECBNSC3i514DrMancwMIBIBIyOg05WO9Qz2ldyOBaZbiuTFgJ52tcEFhsEGvr1X_a1Cu8V9g1-vLY8uxua_vpTTcvd_nAzJbExYbLVA0AJw)]
* AI Metrics: Evaluates various index measurements of AI task exposure across standard occupational classifications. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEShAEB6zswFTsJCpN3LfkWeR8cD8dNHhJ65UXoox0P0ctL-4y_AWwGcYpRMxkwYYZOIfSIK_MK2hEwCnJ_arp7ZOxcqeHijyuQMGTcU_NePeojOiKLw9f7tkBTLs2WVfDDnAY1rsWinK4PIVf723WZByuReArXzgSURiYWLxJsg3rYLP5kqNk), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESewHrOzAVIdVACqsbX8syqbHRyGuC6LUKKtyZ4pvAADg1FMzpd1j7dzdiX8dECBNSC3i514DrMancwMIBIBIyOg05WO9Qz2ldyOBaZbiuTFgJ52tcEFhsEGvr1X_a1Cu8V9g1-vLY8uxua_vpTTcvd_nAzJbExYbLVA0AJw)]
* Comparisons: Analyzes employment, wage, and unemployment trajectories of workers in high- versus low-AI exposure categories. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESewHrOzAVIdVACqsbX8syqbHRyGuC6LUKKtyZ4pvAADg1FMzpd1j7dzdiX8dECBNSC3i514DrMancwMIBIBIyOg05WO9Qz2ldyOBaZbiuTFgJ52tcEFhsEGvr1X_a1Cu8V9g1-vLY8uxua_vpTTcvd_nAzJbExYbLVA0AJw)]
